1.t: Meeting Armstrong in Chicago, 1927, and Chicago's migration scene
1.s: Barker says he got to know Armstrong in 1927 when Lee Collins' band took an excursion to Chicago; he explains the Illinois Central excursions, his Uncle Paul Barberin going to Chicago, and the Great Migration.
1.ch: Armstrong in Chicago
1.q: I knew Louis Armstrong real well. I got known him from around 19... 20... 27 when I went to Chicago. Lee Collins' band went on an excursion from New Orleans, and Lee and Lurie were buddies from kids. And naturally, Louis, Lee searched Lurie out and went to an excursion which they used to give all…

1.t: Astoria band, boyhood Chicago nightlife, and Armstrong borrowing a trumpet
1.s: Barker describes playing with Jones and Collins' Astoria Band, peeking into Chicago cabarets as a boy in 1923, then Armstrong sitting in at the Royal Garden on a borrowed horn and the owner's anger.
1.ch: Armstrong in Chicago
1.q: I was with Lee Collins, Jones and Collins. Astoria Band. We played at Astoria. We played in New Orleans on Rampart Street which was owned by Beansy Furrier. It had once been owned by, I can't think of a man's name. It was a brewery people. Beansy took it over. It was a gambling concession. and we…

1.t: Sugar Johnny, Johnny Dodds and Chicago's New Orleans men
1.s: Musicians visiting home are discussed, including the unrecorded trumpeter Sugar Johnny and Johnny Dodds keeping the New Orleans tradition in Chicago.
1.ch: Old New Orleans musicians and schooling
1.q: Sure. You see them when they leave town. They come to visit, and you don’t know who they are. [? (inaudible)], “Oh, what you say? Man, when you get in town?” Sugar Johnny. I saw him once. Great trumpet player, but you never hear nothing, because he didn’t record. Ain’t got nobody to pull for him. I…

1.t: Chicago excursions and the span of King Oliver's career
1.s: He corrects White about when he went north by rail excursion and reflects on bands' careers lasting about ten years, with Ellington as the exception.
1.ch: Chicago, return and Harlem 1930
1.q: From ’20 to ’30. King Oliver had his career. You have your career in music for a certain length period of time, and then you phase out. Very few bands have kept on persist. There was Duke [Ellington], because he paid his own band out of his own royalties, I think. Should have made, had millions…

1.t: King Oliver's Chicago clubs and the Lincoln Gardens
1.s: Barker never heard Oliver's band in Chicago but later played at the Lincoln Gardens on a New Orleans excursion, noting David Jones and Armstrong's coolness.
1.ch: Chicago, return and Harlem 1930
1.q: As far as me going to the club, I didn’t go. It was Savoy and Royal Gardens. The Royal Gardens is something else. What they call it now? Not the Savoy. It was the Royal Gardens.

1.t: The 1929 Chicago trip and the two Cooks
1.s: He returned to Chicago with Lee Collins and David Jones to play Warrick Hall, hosted by Professor Cook, whom he distinguishes from Doc Cook.
1.ch: Chicago, return and Harlem 1930
1.q: Professor Cook was also a promoter. He was sort of a leader of the black entertainer. Lyric Theater, New Orleans, Rampart Street. Famous Professor Cook.

1.t: Chicago in 1932 with Bud Harris's stranded band
1.s: Danny went to Chicago with vaudeville star Bud Harris's band, stayed at the Ritz, and was blocked from playing the Regal because of house-band rules.
1.ch: A musical family and the old New Orleans bands
1.q: I know. He was nice... And so he knew me. After I met him, he knew me. And then, when I went to Chicago... Let me see, this was '32. I went there with Bud Harris. We stayed at a hotel of that a man owned that owned the Grand Terrace.

1.t: Jack Johnson's nightclub and its gold spittoons
1.s: The boys watched a man polish the spittoons and lay a ruffled rug outside Jack Johnson's club.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: And we walked to 40...34th and...some street which had a nightclub. It was Jack Johnson's nightclub. And he used to put out (?) gold spittoons.

1.t: The Vendome, Grand Theatre and State Street theatres
1.s: Milt and Danny place the Vendome (Erskine Tate) and the Grand (Dave Peyton) on State Street.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: Because they had a lot of...a cluster of theatres around there.

1.t: White Sox Park with Uncle Paul and King Oliver; Black baseball
1.s: Paul took Danny to a White Sox game with King Oliver, and Milt recalls the Colored Giants on 39th Street.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: The commuter trains coming. Well, that was my first taste of Chicago. Then they took us... My Uncle Paul taken us to the ballgame, the White Sox Park, which was on the South Side.

1.t: Sherman Cook the showman, and Milt's memories of him
1.s: Cook was a sharp-dressed, gold-toothed showman who fascinated Milt as a boy because he courted his aunt.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: He put on a show. He was a showman. And he was a showman on and off stage. Because when he wasn't on stage, he had something that denoted that was no working man. He had some kind of sharp costume on, and that cigar.

1.t: Milt's all-star Chicago band with Jabbo Smith and Cassino Simpson
1.s: Milt describes the band assembled to cover Louis's slot at a gangster-owned club, with Simpson, Pasquall, Floyd Campbell and Tinsley.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians

1.s: Jabbo showed up late to the gangsters' club, so Cassino Simpson took over; his tunes were all about soul food.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: [CHUCKLES]

1.t: Charles Elgar's orchestra and Eddie South's planned big band
1.s: Milt describes violinist Charles Elgar and the 1931 big band Elgar organized for Eddie South to play a Chicago hotel.

1.q: To me, Charles Elgar was a very high-class man. He was one of Eddie South's teachers, a great violinist -- Charles Elgar was a violin player. And he had an orchestra, a very good orchestra. Not a Jazz orchestra, from what I can understand, but a dance orchestra that played nightclubs and played…

1.t: Adolphus Allsbrook, the Golden Gloves bassist gambler, in Chicago
1.s: Milt tells of meeting Allsbrook, who asked for lessons, brushed through Milt's book and later beat up muggers in an alley.
1.ch: Danny's rise through New York bands to Cab Calloway
1.q: The first time I saw Adolphus Allsbrook was in Chicago. He came to.... He was a Golden Glove fighter. He was boxing. And he was a converted gambler, just insane for gambling. And he won he Golden Glove contest out there, and

1.t: Jerome Pasquall and Charlie Cooke's band at White City
1.s: Danny and Milt recall Pasquall's work with Fletcher, King Oliver and Charlie Cooke's high-class band at Chicago's White City.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: Jerome Pasquall was one of the masters. He had been with Fletcher, he had been with King Oliver, he had been with that big...that great...Cooke's band... Charlie Cooke.

1.t: Peeping into the morning cabaret on State Street
1.s: The boys lay on their stomachs to look down into a dive where people still danced at eight in the morning; Milt did the same on his paper route.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: Now, there was another little cabaret we used to go and peep around 7 or 7:30, maybe around 8 o'clock in the morning, on State Street. We'd go there and we would lay on our stomach by the side... You'd go in there and you could look down and see these people in there dancing, still having a good…

1.t: First trip to Chicago at ten to join Uncle Paul
1.s: Barker went to Chicago with his grandparents and uncle Willie, hearing speakeasy music and peeping into basement cabarets with Ollie Powers and Tony Jackson.
1.ch: Chicago, return and Harlem 1930
1.q: My uncle Paul Barbarin was with King Oliver. He sent for his mother to come up. She said, “I’ll take Willie.” That’s my uncle. He’s two years older than me. I’m what? 10. Willie’s 12. So I started crying, “I want to go.” So they talked about it. Said all right. You take me too, so there’s two of…

1.t: Charles Elgar's later years and the Chicago union
1.s: Milt recalls Elgar's help to young musicians like Richard Davis, his union offices and his wife living in New York.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: But the people who went through that disappointment, like you said, Charles Elgar and them people, they... I guess they had seen a lot. And he was a high-class man.

1.t: Forgotten Chicago players: Jimmy Strong, Hobson, Reuben Reeves
1.s: Milt and Danny list neglected musicians whose names should be remembered, including a saxophonist who slobbered when he played.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: A cat who looked like Freddie Keppard in Chicago, who was such a terrific trumpet player. Great, big fat guy. They called him Fatso...

1.t: Jimmie Noone and Paul Barbarin married sisters; Noone's 1932 band in New York
1.s: Paul and clarinetist Jimmie Noone married Thomas sisters; Noone came to New York in 1932 with a six-piece band that included Big Green.
1.ch: Lu Barker and the Barbarin family
1.q: A little quiet saxophone player who later went to Milwaukee. He lived in Milwaukee, and he had a pressing business in Milwaukee. That's standard now.

1.t: Bill Bottoms of the Royal Garden and King Jones, the first MC
1.s: Danny recalls the Chicago manager Bill Bottoms and MC King Jones, who introduced King Oliver and Freddie Keppard as two kings on one throne.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: King Jones used to announce King Oliver and Freddie Keppard, who at one period they both played in the band together. He said, "Two kings on one throne. First time you ever seen that, la-deez on..." Paul used to laugh. He said, "La-deez on gentleman." And these ladies were sitting on (?), grabbing…

1.t: The Monogram theatre and Jack Johnson's Stutz
1.s: Milt recalls the Monogram vaudeville house and staring at Jack Johnson's open Stutz car.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: Yeah, yeah, he was something. Yeah, that Chicago was something.

1.t: Lee Collins's band and the Illinois Central excursion to Chicago
1.s: Lee Collins's band, Danny's first, went on the weekend excursion train from New Orleans to Chicago for Professor Cook.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: The excursion came up... Like, they used to have an excursion from New Orleans and other parts on the I.C. It was nine hundred miles from New Orleans to Chicago, and they would give you weekend excursions to Chicago at a

1.t: Dave Peyton and the classical musicians who hated jazz
1.s: Milt describes Dave Peyton of the Grand Theatre, anti-jazz and classical-trained, whom Paul Barbarin arranged for.
1.ch: Cab Calloway, Harlem and New York musicians
1.q: And it made 'em mo' mad when they had some of these raggedy sumbitches from all over the country, out of St. Louis, playing this funky music in them dives and tonks, and they become celebrated. Because the mass of the people dug that kind of music. See, and they all...

8.t: Assembling the Oliver band and hiring Lil Hardin
8.s: For the Royal Garden he recruited Joe Oliver, Johnny Dodds, Mutt Carey, Norah, Minor Hall, and borrowed pianist Lil Hardin from Mrs. Jones's music store.
8.q: Royal Garden. And he wants some music, you know. Well, I said, it's a good chance for us to get our old band together. I said, yeah, I'll send for Joe Oliver. Can you get him? I said, sure, I can get him. All right, I'll send for Joe Oliver. That's Joe Oliver. Johnny Dodds come in with Mac and Mac.…

8.t: Booking at the music store and the band's lineup
8.s: The store booked bands; he lists the band he put together with Oliver and notes that the piano replaced the guitar.
8.q: They used to book bands and they used to send people on jobs, you know. Yeah, in private. So you see, they'd send you on jobs.

8.t: West side jobs and the Ansonia with Perez
8.s: He recalls the Chinese restaurant job and Madison Street, and the Ansonia with Perez, Teo, Cantrell and Frank Aime.
8.q: I was over on the west side, yeah. I was over on, I think I was over on Madison. I was over on Madison, some left in there, Palina, Madison Palina. And we all played up there, Madison Palina, at the Sonia with myself, Emmanuel Perez, Teo, Lorenzo Teo, Cantrell, Frank Aime, and Dixieland, and the…

8.s: After the Dreamland they played the Pekin until morning; he recalls McCurdy's disappearance, Piku and Dave Payton's band.
8.q: Yeah. Then when they come back, we left there, then I had Manuel with me over in the Deluxe. Then I had a job playing down at the Pekin. That's 28th and the State. Yeah. It was an old Pekin Theater.

8.s: After coming back to Chicago he led a band with Manuel Perez, Eddie Atkins, Lorenzo Tio, Frankie Haine and Louis Cottrell.
8.ch: Chicago and Oliver's band in California
8.q: No, not too much about them. Mm-hmm. I don't know quite a few of them. He left and come home back to Chicago. I hadn't played with me a while in Chicago.

8.t: The Deluxe on 35th and State, Chicago
8.s: Garland starts at the Deluxe, upstairs on 35th and State, and describes the Blue Monday custom, the room and the competition with Billy Bottoms and Dreamland.
8.q: I went to Mabel Elaine, the show. Then we come back to Chicago, later on Chicago there, for a while, you understand. We got to go around different nightclubs, so they heard about the band. I went to work. Oh, you know, they got over there what they call Blue Mondays, Blue Wednesdays. Every…

8.t: Three or four years at the Deluxe with Garland's New Orleans Jazz Band
8.s: He stays at the Deluxe until Billy Bottoms lures him to Dreamland, and recalls stealing a touring act's player for the Deluxe. The band was Garland's New Orleans Jazz Band.
8.q: Oh, I stayed, I stayed, I stayed in the Deluxe three, four years or more. Then, two years and something. Because Billy Bottoms got me to come over to Dreamland, see. Just before I went to the Dreamland, uh, Basie come to Chicago with, uh, P.R. this woman who called, oh, it was already a TV time,…

8.t: Building the band: Dodds, Dutrey, Tubby Hall, Minor Hall, Lil Hardin
8.s: Garland lists how he gathered Johnny Dodds, Noah Dutrey, the Hall brothers and Lil Hardin, with Joe Oliver coming in. The transcript has an ASR loop of 'Oakland' in the middle.
8.q: Then, uh, Johnny Dodds come in town. We got a hold of Johnny Dodds. Nora Dutre was in the neighborhood. He used to come into Chicago and he'd come sit in with us. So, uh, Boyd H. Williams opened up the, uh, the, opened up this club on 34th Street, uh, Oakland And Joe comes in, all right? Joe gets…

8.t: Other New Orleans men in Chicago: Big Eye Louis, Baquet, Dreamland bands
8.s: Later bands that followed the Creole Band to Chicago, and Garland's own bands at Dreamland with Lorenzo Tio on clarinet.
8.q: Then the next band went, Big Eye Lewy. He come along. Big Eye Lewy was with Freddie and, uh, and-and-and-and George Backe was with, uh, And, uh, George Fields was with Manuel. Then when I was at the Dreamland, I went to Wake Down and Peekin for Dan Jackson, and I used to have Manuel, Teo, Frankie…

8.t: Half-Pint Jackson and leaving Chicago in 1920
8.s: A question about Frankie Half-Pint Jackson, then Garland gives 1920 as when he left Chicago with the Oliver band.

8.t: Chicago jobs: the luncheonette and Manuel Perez's band
8.s: After the show closed he played for Isadora Shaw, then with Perez at Paulina and Madison where two bands shared a gangster-run house.
8.q: And I played out there with him. And he had Manuel Perez played trumpet. Eddie Atkins playing trombone. Lorenzo To playing clarinet.

8.t: Freddie Keppard and Garland's own Chicago band
8.s: Keppard joined Garland's Chicago band when Sugar Johnny fell ill; Garland names Palmer, Duke Dewey, Lil Hardin and Tubby Hall, then turned the band over to Dewey.
8.q: Oh, yeah. When he come to Chicago -- when he come back from New York to come back to Chicago, he was playing with this girl that I went to play with, May Elaine.

8.t: Manuel Perez as a sweet player and Chicago's welcome for New Orleans music
8.s: Perez was a sweet, not hot, trumpeter and Tea did the hot playing; Chicago audiences loved New Orleans music.
8.q: He played a lot of trumpet but he wasn't no hot man, no.

8.s: Garland thinks he knew Horace Eubanks in Chicago, and the interviewer discusses what little is known of him.
8.q: He played here. I was Fountain Blue. He played here on the boat.

58.t: Opening; arriving in Chicago in 1927 with the Miramakers show
58.s: Allen opens the session; Punch recounts reaching Chicago with a traveling show and settling with Al Wynn, Tiny Parham, Hughie Swift and Francois's band at the Golden Lily.
58.q: Well, I went in there with a big show from traveling on the road in the year of 1927. And the show was named the Miramak Miramakers. And after I got in Chicago, well, I struck all, struck luck there with fellas like Al Wynn, Tiny Palm, and Hughie Swift and all them kind of fellas. And I just got…

58.t: First Chicago jobs: Al Wynn, the Bookstore, Huey Swift
58.s: Punch lists his first Chicago bands: Al Wynn at the Dreamland, a four-piece at the Bookstore, then Huey Swift at the Jeffery Club.
58.q: Well, I don't know, me and Cliff Jones on drums, and some other guys, I can't remember them fellas now. Been a good while, you know.

58.t: Tiny Parham and Al Wynn at the Dreamland; the recordings
58.s: Sorting out the sequence of bands, Punch explains the twelve-piece Dreamland band run by Wynn and Parham, who made records and shared men.
58.q: Tiny Palm was after Francois? No, Tiny Palm was a little before Francois. See, I don't know if it, I don't know if it was Tiny Palm Band or Al when band, but they both was there together. See, you know, I think it was Tiny Palm, but Al when was doing a lot of managing, you know. But I'm pretty sure…

58.s: Punch says he did not work with either Doc Cook but did play jobs with Jimmy Noone in Chicago.
58.q: In Chicago. I worked at Tipus Inn with him. Worked white club with him a couple of nights like that.

58.t: Tommy Ladnier and Joe Alba known only in Chicago
58.s: Miller says he first saw Ladnier and a second musician in Chicago and comments on their records.
58.q: No, I heard of him when I got in Chicago. To tell the truth, I saw him. But he left and went to England or somewhere while I was there.

58.t: Drummers with Oliver, Morton and Hilaire; Jeffery Tavern band
58.s: They discuss the drummer's employers and Hilaire, who played in Chicago with Jimmy Noone.
58.q: King Oliver, General Morton, and a fella you don't know of. Huey Swift. He was the first Negro band in Chicago that went on the air. First one. He had a beat playing. I was good at him. Jeffery Tavern, the name was Jeffery Tavern, South Chicago and Jeffery. And the car dope, and the place closed it…

58.t: Chicago audiences compared to New Orleans
58.s: Punch says Chicago liked blues at first and later classic music.
58.q: I see. Did they have the same kind of dancing in Chicago they used to have down here? When I first went there, yeah, they was doing the same thing. Same thing.

58.t: I Won't Give You None and Jimmy Bertrand
58.s: Allen and Punch try to place the song on the back of Isabella and meeting Bertrand at the Regal.
58.q: I Don't Know. I Don't Know. I Don't Know. It's on the back of which one? Isabella. Well that was with Billy Macanick, wasn't it? Jimmy Bertrand.

58.t: The Bookstore job and Junie Cobb's recommendation to Hughie Swift
58.s: Punch recounts Tenny Wilson's wife getting him a job at the Bookstore, Junie Cobb hiring him, and a federal raid.
58.q: That's the man who got me the job at Jeffrey Tabin. Two brothers, Junie Cobb and Jimmy Cobb. I was playing after, this was before I went to Golden Lily though, I just went to Chicago with the show, Mac and Mac. And we was playing at a little place called Bookstore. I tell you, her wife was playing…

58.t: Eddie Carl and the Carnes brothers
58.s: Punch identifies Eddie Carl, trumpeter, and Eddie and Zinke Carnes, pianists, and the union president Arch Joe.
58.q: Well, he was on the, what do you know, he played on that show too. But I mean, I wasn't there when he played there, but I played with him with the Royal American show. Eddie Carl, trauma player, good old, good musician, man. He used to read, you sit down there and read the trumpet parts. Look over…

58.t: Jimmy Wade and the Isabella record with Francois Luzan
58.s: Punch recalls the Wade band, the Isabella record and drummer Francois's club singing of a greasy pole song.
58.q: Well, Jimmy Wade had some fellas, no you asked me that once before Dick, but I swear I can't remember them fellas. I can't remember.

455.s: Budd and Hinton rehearse daily and play a roadhouse with Tick Gray; Hinton's mother refuses to let him go to Milwaukee.

455.q: Way out of town, yeah, and we had our -- we had a good little group. But Everett Barksdale was in Chicago at that time, and --

455.s: Floyd Campbell hires Budd for the Panama on "Dodge City" 58th Street, with Gideon Honore and Jabo Smith.

455.s: Musicians walk daily from the Michigan Hotel to the union hall, where Tubby Hall cooks red beans and rice, and Budd mentions a photo of Ben Webster.
455.q: I believe his last name was Washington too. But any way we used to walk -- Bob Red Cross had a little pad at the Michigan Hotel.

455.s: Budd names Leon Washington, Boyd Atkins, Omer Simeon, Cecil Irvin and Doll Hutchison in Chicago.

455.q: Boyd Atkins -- of course, you know Omar Simson and Darnell played a lot of clarinet and violin. Of course, they were with Earl. I hadn't -- I used to hear them all the time, but I hadn't joined the band at that time. And, Cecil Irving played very good tenor. And --

455.s: Back in Chicago Budd plays at the Savoy with Horace Henderson, a great arranger now raising horses in Colorado.

455.s: Budd likens Scoops Cary and Del Bright to Charlie Parker and recalls Jerome Pasquall, Dave Young, Ray Nance's band and Leroy Harris.

77.t: Upstairs at the Panama, then Frank Peer's Deluxe with Noone and Keppard
77.s: Singing blues upstairs at the Panama with other singers while stars come to listen, pianist George Hall, then next door to the Deluxe with Jimmy Noone and Freddie Keppard.

77.t: White audiences and Dreamland as Chicago's fanciest club
77.s: Theaters and Chicago after-hours spots were crowded with white patrons; Dreamland was the biggest and fanciest, with its glass floor, ahead of the Sunset.
77.q: Yeah, you could hardly get in any of those theaters for the white people. Yeah, most of the time it was no place for the colored ones. And especially -- that's another thing about Chicago, you couldn't get in those places for the white people -- in the after hour places, especially. See. No, you…

77.t: Hunter's own chronology of clubs, recordings and shows
