77.ch: Struttin' Time, chronology and Chicago singers
77.q: Oh, yeah, uh-huh. Well, this was way -- Now, listen -- another thing. What did I see -- oh, let me see whether I -- I think I've got something here that'll help you out too, Chris. Oh, Lord, all this rattling on there.

77.t: Ranking Chicago clubs and the Panama's singers
77.s: Dreamland first, the Grand Terrace second; the Panama had two floors with Florence Mills, Bricktop, Cora Green and Mattie Hite.
77.ch: Struttin' Time, chronology and Chicago singers
77.q: Let me see, the Panama had two floors, but Panama, it was just a little club. Of course, it was lovely, but I mean it wasn't -- nothing fancy like the Dreamland.

77.t: Her own list of Chicago jobs before New York
77.s: Reading her notes she lists the Regal Theater, Packy McFarland's, Burnham Inn and Dreamland before moving to New York.
77.ch: New Orleans musicians, recordings and radio
77.q: Just told you, yeah, Burnham Inn. And during that time recorded; of course, I was still at the Dreamland. World War I I was at the Dreamland.

77.t: The De Luxe owned by Frank Preer, husband of Evelyn Preer
77.s: After the Panama she went next door to Frank Preer's De Luxe, where Freddie Keppard played.
77.q: Because -- oh, Frank Preer (PHONETIC) owned the De Luxe. And I went to the De Luxe and that's where Freddy Keppard (PHONETIC) was.

77.t: Who the customers were at each club
77.s: Hoskins was mostly Black; the Elite somewhat mixed; the Panama loaded with whites from downtown and the West Side; Dago Frank's all white except pianist Bruce.
77.q: -- it was mixed. Not much. White fellows, a white person would come in in the Elite. But I don't remember the whites mixing down in Hoskin's, Hugh Hoskin's.

77.t: Dreamland food, Ollie Powers and May Alix taking her job
77.s: She also doubled at after-hours clubs; Bottoms ran a first-class kitchen; she worked with tenor Ollie Powers and left her job to May Alix, a stockyards worker.
77.q: Getting very close to it, though, because when I -- when I -- while I was working at Dreamland I worked at the -- I mean, when I left Dreamland I worked at a little old club over there on Wabash. No, I don't want to bring that, because that's when I left and came right straight to New York. I…

77.t: After-hours places where Black performers gathered; kindred feeling with the band
77.s: Performers went to hear one another at after-hours spots like the Pekin, celebrities packed in, and musicians picked up songs they hummed.
77.ch: Records, Lovie Austin and a first marriage
77.q: Yes. Yes. For instance, now, every [Pekin] time after I'd leave my work at night, I'd go to the Peek-in or whatever after hour place it was, but usually I'd be working at those places. But most of the other artists would come in to listen to -- not just me, but whatever artist would be there, you…

77.t: The Dreamland balcony and glass floor
77.s: Louis and the band were up high on a platform; Hunter identifies a photograph as Dreamland with its balcony and glass floor.
77.q: Up high. They were up high, up there like that. And we were down here. But they would be way up like that ceiling. Uh-huh. Big, big platform.

378.t: The Three Spooks and a paid trip to Chicago
378.s: At the station he led a piano, alto and xylophone trio; the manager grants two weeks' paid travel, and he describes the Marigold band's musicians.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: Yeah, and John Wald came in after -- and funny, this Jack Tiboo got him a job with WGN. But I'm getting ahead of my story --

378.t: Victor Young hires him for the Maytag program
378.s: Walking down Randolph Street he meets Victor Young, who has been seeking a jazz xylophonist for the Maytag show; they had met at the Uptown Theater.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: Yeah, but they wouldn't leave town. They liked it there. Anyway, I went to Chicago and I'm walking down Randolph Street and I walk into Victor Young. And that's when he started up --

378.t: Ben Bernie at the College Inn; Whiteman hears him
378.s: He works with Ben Bernie's band at the Sherman's College Inn doing solos; Whiteman hears him play 'In a Mist' alone and hires him for NBC.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: And I never went back to Minneapolis. And, from that -- I don't know I was around there and I did some things with Ben Bernie, was -- so when he went in the College Inn, I went in with him, with Dick Stabile and all these people that was with Ben Bernie.

378.t: NBC Merchandise Mart with Jules Herbuveaux; the Wingy Manone show
378.s: Whiteman puts him on staff with Jules Herbuveaux's group and he also leads an early-morning jazz show with Wingy Manone, Volly De Faut and Dave Rose.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: So, we were like the Blue Blazers in the afternoon, we're the Tea -- I mean the morning, the Blue Blazers in the afternoon. --

378.t: Meeting Mildred and backing the afternoon shows
378.s: At NBC Chicago his band accompanies Mildred, Johnny Fulton and the new Rhythm Boys; he tells her he first heard her on the radio.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: -- they had taken studios there. So, but those two shows, the people like [Senkeny,] and Robb and people who were head of NBC in Chicago, at that time, Whiteman just put me right in with Jules. We had a six -- I guess it was six-seven piece band. And we just -- piano, bass and drums and all that…

378.t: Courtship in Chicago: dinners and hearing Hines and Ellington
378.s: He and Mildred begin going out after work to hear Earl Hines, Duke Ellington and others; Ted Pearson and Don Bernard are part of the circle.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: During that time, cause then, I don't know, we did something that band with Mildred, and I forgot what it was, now I don't -- can't put my hand on it. But we did some kind of a little show.

378.t: NBC staff band; hearing Duke and Teddy Wilson
378.s: As Whiteman's NBC musical director in Chicago employed him, he and Mildred heard Duke Ellington and Teddy Wilson; they later recognized Wilson in New York.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: I did a couple of those and so I would just go and I used to go over and pick up Mildred there, maybe some of us would go out to the Dells or someplace like that near -- to hear Duke or Tom Geroni or some of the bands that would come into Chicago.

378.t: The Blackhawk in Chicago; Mildred joins the band
378.s: Don Roth books the band into the Blackhawk, and Mildred joins the broadcasts; they become Mr. and Mrs. Swing.
378.ch: New York bands and the first records
378.q: way or the other. Finally when they -- finally they said, well we'll put her in the show with Ronald Vincent. With a dance team. Now, we had -- still had the little singer, Nancy Flake --

378.t: First solo with Paul Ash's band at the Oriental
378.s: Paul Ash's stage band at the Oriental Theater, a jazz-friendly outfit with singers like Ruth Etting, gave Norvo his first solo with a band.
378.ch: Chicago radio, Whiteman and courting Mildred
378.q: So anyway we went to the thing and the guy heard us and so he said, well there's an opening with Paul Ash, for the opening show at the Oriental. So, I -- he booked me on it. Now Paul saw me and he okayed the idea that we'd try a solo with him and that's the first time I did it with a band.

166.t: Chicago: Lil Armstrong, Roy Eldridge and Art Tatum
166.s: His first Chicago job was with Lil Armstrong, where he met Roy Eldridge and sat in at the Three Deuces with Tatum.
166.ch: First bass jobs in California, Chicago and the move to New York
166.q: And my first job was with Lil Armstrong. And she was on one end -- we were playing the Bacon's Casino. And she was on one end of the bandstand, and the tenor player and the trumpet player and the drummer player was over on the other end of the bandstand. So I'm standing up there by her.

166.t: Chicago bandleaders and clubs after Les Wilcox
166.s: He lists the Chicago leaders he worked for, starting with Les Wilcox, and the Club De Luxe.
166.ch: First bass jobs in California, Chicago and the move to New York
166.q: So Roy said (unintelligible). I went up to the bandstand, took the base. First note, Art got up, he didn't have to look up, he knew who it was. So I stayed around there, and I worked with a wonderful musician, a bandleader, four pieces combo -- Les Wilcox. He could write and arrange individual…

166.t: Roy Eldridge at the Capitol Lounge and the tune that became 'Ball of Fire'
166.s: Roy opened downtown despite Petrillo; a tune Roy and Claxton wrote was renamed 'Ball of Fire' for Krupa.
166.ch: First bass jobs in California, Chicago and the move to New York
166.q: Now, the local Negroes couldn't work in the Loop without Petrillo's permission. He wasn't about to give his permission, even some of the jobs on the West Side we had to petition for, to get his permission. So Roy says, "I'm opening at the Capital Lounge." That was right next door to the Capital…

166.t: First jobs in Chicago: Tiny Parham, Lee Collins and Calumet City
166.s: He found work through Tiny Parham, with Lil Hardin and with Erskine Tate, Lee Collins and Sonny Thompson in Calumet City for small pay.
166.ch: Records, Blanton, the Chicago scene, Nat Cole and Nadine
166.q: And I got to Chicago, and this fellow, Tiny Parham, he was a huge man. And he played organ in the Savoy Ballroom. For the skaters, and pre-prize fights, you know, like organists play for ball games and things like that? He was the house band. He played the organ there all the time. However, he…

166.t: Playing with Punch Miller, Charles Elgar and Rip Bassett
166.s: Names the older Chicago players he worked with.
166.ch: Records, Blanton, the Chicago scene, Nat Cole and Nadine
166.q: Then I worked -- not for, but with the legendary Punch Miller, with the All Stars on 43rd Street in Chicago. I forget who had the band, but he would always -- he was a fixture there. He'd play there all the time. But I never knew that Punch had the historic background that he had till this book…

166.t: Eddie South, and Earl Hines hidden behind a screen
166.s: Praises violinist Eddie South; Willard adds Hines' story of being screened from view.
166.ch: Records, Blanton, the Chicago scene, Nat Cole and Nadine
166.q: Now, there's a name for you. Eddie South was equipped for symphony, but he was ahead of his time. He had studied abroad and everything. But he played modern jazz as well. So he played better jazz on the violin than any violinist, including Joe Venuti, Stuff Smith, any of the rest of them. Because…

166.s: Calumet City was like 52nd Street, with steady white bands and weekend jobs for Black groups.
166.ch: Records, Blanton, the Chicago scene, Nat Cole and Nadine
166.q: No it was a weekend situation; but the ones that were steady were caucasians, you know. When they wanted a black ethnic group. it was weekend, like Saturday night, you know.

166.t: Follow-ups on Chicago: Lil Armstrong, Club Deluxe, Ray Nance and the Swingland
166.s: Clarifies the one-night Lil Armstrong job, Joe Hughes' Club De Luxe, and where he heard Ray Nance.
166.ch: Clarifications and portraits: Lester Young, Byas, Blanton, Ben Webster
166.q: Yeah, I heard Ray Nance when Earl Hines came out here to Los Angeles before I ever left here. He and Trummy Young was with the Band. And they were featured instrumentalist and singers with the band at that time.

166.t: Follow-ups: Marlowe Morris, Chicago leaders Dickerson, Tate, Punch Miller, Elgar, and the
166.s: Short portraits of the pianist and the Chicago bandleaders; asks about a poll.
166.ch: Clarifications and portraits: Lester Young, Byas, Blanton, Ben Webster
166.q: He was a pianist. A very good pianist. He played more on the stride type of piano playing. Using his left hand, you know. But if you had to swing, he could do that too. He could play some beautiful ballads.

239.t: Stuff Smith Trio in Chicago: Three Deuces and the Garrick Lounge
239.s: Clubs where the trio worked, and Jones's brief stint with Red Allen at the Garrick Lounge.
239.q: Yeah. The Three Deuces, which was in the Loop, on Wabash Avenue, and the Garrick Lounge, which was on Randolph. And the Garrick Lounge was a very special kind of a place. It was an upstairs and a downstairs. I worked with Red Allen in the Garrick Lounge too. With Higginbottom (PHO1 ham NETC). Yeah,…

239.t: Other Chicago music around the Garrick Lounge
239.s: Eddie South, Billy Taylor and Pete Brown nearby, and the Garrick's layout; Stuff Smith not getting his due.
239.q: I don't think he ever got his due credit, but I don't think he allowed himself to get it. He would go off and chase ladies and wouldn't settle down completely to his

239.t: Ray Nance at the Garrick Lounge and Randolph Street clubs
239.s: Correcting the earlier tape: Ray Nance played the Garrick in the 1940s during a layoff from Duke, and Roy Eldridge played across the street.
239.q: He just came home and there he was, and he was available to play up to a certain point, when the band went on the road, when Duke went back out on the road. The six pieces, that goes way back into his young years.

239.t: Chicago clubs compared with New York's 52nd Street
239.s: About twenty Chicago clubs near the Three Deuces; Chicago rooms were softer and more midwestern than New York cellars.
239.q: Oh, I'm trying to remember where Eddie South and Billy Taylor were working. They had a trio together. As did Stuff and John Levy. Oh, boy, wait a minute. It was in the area of like the Three Deuces in Chicago, the early Three Deuces, where Art Tatum used to work, and where John Collins worked with…

239.t: Roy Eldridge's band across from the Garrick Lounge
239.s: Pianist Rozelle Gayle and Joe Eldridge were in the small Roy Eldridge band.
239.ch: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
239.q: Well, he was a fine pianist. Still is. And he's -- he's turned out to be a fine actor on television, you know.

239.t: Meeting John Levy in 1937 in Tony Fambro's band
239.s: Playing piano in Tony Fambro's Chicago band that battled Nat Cole's orchestra, then the trip to Indianapolis and stranding.
239.ch: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
239.q: Oh, let's see. 1937, I can tell you. We were working with a local band and I was called in to play piano in this particular band because -- the name of the band was the Tony [Fanborough](PHONETIC), and they used to have battles of jazz with the Nat Cole Orchestra. And Nat had a big band, you know.…

239.t: Tony Fambro's band, its Ellington sound and Duke raiding its men
239.s: Fambro's eight-piece band was called Little Duke; Sax Mallard and Nat Jones were taken by Ellington; John Levy played bass.
239.q: Yeah, but at that time they had stopped having those battles of the bands. I joined [Fambro] (PHONETIC) after that, but I used to be around -- hang around the bandstand to listen to them.

239.t: How long Fambro's band lasted and Duke taking its men
239.s: Jones was with Fambro's Ellington-oriented band about three years; Nat Jones and Sax Mallard drifted back from Ellington.
239.ch: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
239.q: Let me see. Now, John Levy probably would know this, because John was playing bass with it. I guess I was with Tony[Fambreau's]band about three years or so, you know.

239.t: Ray Nance's early violin sextet in Chicago
239.s: Ray Nance was a Chicago star leading a six-piece band with three doubling violinists before joining Duke.
239.q: I knew him, yeah. But I -- you know, in those days Ray Nance was one of the Chicago stars, if you want to put it that way. Even though he didn't act like it. He was never arrogant. But Ray was one of the -- he had one of the nicest little six pieces, you know. All three of them in the front line…

22.t: Harry James and taking a band to Chicago in 1916
22.s: Impresario Harry James hired him to furnish a band, taken to Chicago in March 1916.
22.q: Well, I was playing on a court here on Canal Street, and Harry James is an impresario. He heard me play, and he asked me if I could furnish him a band. So at this time, I used to play at the Old Haymarket, and they had several men playing that I knew, and we formed that band and brought that band…

22.t: Article continued: Chicago swing bands and King Oliver's wah-wah
22.s: The article names the Creole Band, King Oliver and Chicago bands c. 1917; La Rocca doubts Oliver invented the wah-wah.
22.ch: Clarence Williams's 1936 article and the dispute
22.q: I thought it was Celestine invented that. That's what they said, Celestine invented that. Clyde McCoy used it. Now King Oliver invented it.

22.t: La Rocca: jazz was born in Chicago, and attacks on rival bands
22.s: La Rocca says the band changed ragtime rhythm in Chicago in 1916, that New Orleans had no jazz, and that Armstrong and the NORK copied the ODJB.
22.ch: La Rocca on who created jazz
22.q: And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed…

22.t: New Orleans bands failing in Chicago and the Schiller Cafe
22.s: He names New Orleans bands that failed in Chicago and describes how dancers' response made jazz at the Schiller Cafe.
22.q: New Rock, Freddie New Rock. Go right in here. There was Judy Stevens, Rag Baby Stevens, and the Berenson brothers. What were their names? Doc Berenson and Benny Berenson. I don't know Doc's name.

22.t: Drummers and the Casino Gardens job
22.s: Earl Carter fills in for Sbarbaro, and Harry James offers $75 a week at Casino Gardens.
22.q: Earl Carter. Yeah. A Chicago drummer. He filled in for two weeks. And Spobara comes up and takes his place. This man knew that that's all the way we used him for two weeks. And we did pretty good at the Del Abbey. Then Harry James buys an entrance in the Casino Gardens with Aikenbar and Reeves. And…

22.t: Averty's December 1956 letter: Melbourne, Johnny Stein, and Brown's 1951 interview begins
22.s: Averty writes from Paris about his travels, correspondence with Stein, Morez and others, and begins quoting Tom Brown's Record Changer story of Frisco and Loretta McDermott and the 1915 Chicago trip.
22.ch: Averty's letters and Tom Brown's claims

22.t: Brown's band lineup, Chicago failure, and New Orleans recruiting in Exchange Alley
22.s: La Rocca lists Brown's players, says they were part fakers and ragtime and made no success in Chicago, and describes bands recruited from Exchange Alley for circuses and road shows before Brown.
22.ch: Tom Brown's band and the first Dixieland claim
22.q: I admitted to you that Brown's band went to Chicago before we did. The people didn't notice them any different. They made no success. So I can't see where they introduced anything. They had many bands like I told you before in the Orangewood's Clarence.

22.t: Brown's account of Lamb's Cafe and the name 'jazz', and Averty's critique
22.s: Brown's quoted account of Lamb's Cafe in 1915, the union and the word jazz, his tour, claims about Tiger Rag; Averty's analysis begins.
22.ch: Averty's letters and Tom Brown's claims

504.t: Chicago musicians who influenced him, Joe Segal and Wilbur Campbell
504.s: He lists Chicago greats, the Jazz Showcase, and Wilbur Campbell's fluid "Chicago swing" drumming.
504.ch: Faith, study and the Chicago scene
504.q: So Chicago is really noted for a lot of great local musicians. Sid Catlett, Ike Day. You had a legendary drummer, Wilbur Campbell, a bass player named Rafael Garrett who was really originally Donald Garrett and later changed to Rafael Garrett. Nicky Hill, a fantastic alto/tenor player and Ira…

504.s: Maurice White played drums in his trio and later visited him in New York on the way to California.
504.ch: Faith, study and the Chicago scene
504.q: Verdine. They used to… …Maurice was pulling out all the sessions. He used to do a lot of the Chess sessions. So he used to do a lot of stuff. He came from the South, I think from Memphis or… …was he from Memphis? One of the cities down South, I forgot where it was. He came up and he used to play…

504.t: Steve McCall, Scotty Holt, Marshall Thompson and Ernest McCarty
504.s: Other Chicago players and mentors he worked with when playing piano.
504.ch: Faith, study and the Chicago scene
504.q: Yeah. Steve used to play with me when I played piano in Chicago also. Steve and Scotty Holt, the bassist who taught me a lot about learning the words to the songs I was playing, get the spiritual thing out of it. He later came to New York, which we'll talk about later when I come to New York. But…

504.t: Von Freeman, Fathers and Sons, Fred Anderson and the Chicago connection
504.s: Playing with Von Freeman at the Jazz Showcase and on Fathers and Sons, and memories of Fred Anderson.
504.q: Yeah, it was and it was formed again when I came back to Chicago and played Joe Segal’s Jazz Showcase. I had a band that was made up of Larry Gray on bass, a very fantastic bassist who plays with Ramsey. Larry Gray, the legendary Jodie Christian on piano, and Ira Sullivan. I did a week with Von…

504.t: Muhal Richard Abrams, the Experimental Orchestra and the AACM
504.s: He left Chicago the year before the AACM formed but played in Abrams's Experimental Orchestra and still works with its members.
504.q: Well it wasn’t the AACM when I was there. I left the year before the AACM was formed. But the year before that one of my mentors, Muhal Richard Abrams formed the, oh what was it – the Orchestra — Experimental Orchestra. So Roscoe and Joseph Jarman and Malachi Favors, we were all sort of playing in…

504.t: Playing with Sun Ra's Arkestra in Chicago
504.s: He rehearses and gigs with Sun Ra at the Wonder Inn, recalls the band, costumes and the pay.
504.q: bands. In that period I got the opportunity… I guess, I'll go back a little bit when I guess I'd left home for a while and I was living on my own and I started working with Sun Ra and his Arkestra at a place called the Wonder Inn. Sun Ra used to rehearse there all the time. At the time the band was…

504.t: Clearing up when he first played with Lester Bowie
504.s: Brown checks the biography: he knew of Bowie in Chicago but first played with him in New York.
504.q: I had heard of him, but I didn’t actually play with him until New York.

504.t: Art Ensemble of Chicago, Robert Crowder and the St. Louis players
504.s: He explains the Art Ensemble and Air formed after he left, and the St. Louis BAG musicians who joined later.
504.q: No. I don't remember hearing Robert with the group. When I heard it I was already in New York, and they had already established themselves with putting paint on their faces and everything.

400.t: Walter Barnes's band and the Chicago scene around 1929
400.s: Hinton recalls Walter Barnes, a Vicksburg clarinetist whose band played the Al Capone Cotton Club, and the 1929 shift in Chicago music.
400.ch: Chicago childhood: theaters, violin and first bass
400.q: Yeah. I remember later in Chicago, one the big bands that came out of that era was the Walter Barnes band. Walter Barnes was from Vicksburg, Mississippi. In fact he went to my mother… he was a boyfriend of my mother‟s youngest sister and he was the one… I‟ve got some wonderful tapes here on Ed…

400.t: Earl Hines at the Grand Terrace and Capone's Cotton Club
400.s: Hines had the first big band working in a club at the Grand Terrace, followed by gangster-run Cotton Club in Cicero.
400.ch: Chicago childhood: theaters, violin and first bass
400.q: Yeah. There were a couple of guys that played in a dancehall, a couple of bands that would… not to really note. Jimmy Bell was one that played at the Savoy Ballroom and places like that but Earl Hines got the Grand Terrace, and Ed Fox…

400.t: Playing the 1933 Democratic Convention hotel fountain
400.s: Eddie South's group plays in the Congress Hotel lobby fountain during the convention that nominated Roosevelt.
400.ch: Eddie South, high school and the South Side scene
400.q: Yeah. We couldn‟t go to hear them but of course they could come to hear us. But the awareness was there. That‟s where Eddie started to really get some popularity. That‟s… what did I say, 1935? No, „32, because 1933 the Democratic Convention was held at the Congress Hotel in Chicago. That was the…

400.t: Tape change, the Austin High group and after-hours jam sessions on the South Side
400.s: White players came to the South Side after hours and both sides learned; Hinton recalls Budd and Keg Johnson, and his mother refusing a Milwaukee job.
400.ch: Capone's Chicago, the union and hired by Cab
400.q: That‟s absolutely right. Benny Goodman especially mentions it but as I said, we‟d meet… that greater south was waiting for [Unintelligible] the Club Ruby [unintelligible] Dixie Beal and [unintelligible] to come to here. They could come any place to hear us but we couldn‟t come any place to hear…

400.t: Truck Parham and the south and west sides of Chicago
400.s: Hinton recalls Truck, his contemporary, and contrasts the south side with the west side's musicians.
400.q: Yeah, Truck was there. There was a big decisions as to whether I taught Truck or whether Truck taught me. We were the same age and we would recollect together. His recording was the one that blossomed out. We were all over his, on the west side. And Chicago was —

400.t: Chicago's isolation as a creative advantage
400.s: Taylor and Hinton note that because black performers returned to the community, young people had access to them.
400.ch: Cotton Club, Zutty and Chicago traditions
400.q: That‟s good, that‟s right. That‟s right, that‟s beautiful. It was a wonderful era to grow up in, to see that Chicago because it was isolated, which we don‟t want anymore, but it was isolated enough where you had to do something.

400.t: Breakfast dances and other places to hear music on the South Side
400.s: Taylor asks where music was heard; Hinton describes breakfast dances that ran from Saturday night to Sunday noon at clubs like the Sunset.
400.ch: Eddie South, high school and the South Side scene
400.q: Well the breakfast dances, the breakfast dances were a big thing. Saturday night… it went late Saturday night until noon Sunday morning and these were clubs on the south side, black clubs where black people went to. The Sunset was a club where black people could go even though it was owned Joe…

400.t: The Vendome versus the Grand: Erskine Tate and Dave Payton
400.s: The Vendome Theater had Louis Armstrong and Eddie South, while Dave Payton's Grand stayed anti-jazz and concert-minded, which Taylor links to color prejudice.
400.ch: Chicago childhood: theaters, violin and first bass
400.q: The black theater and it was just fabulous. Across the street was the Grand Theater that had Dave Payton but they were more classical, they were more minstrel type of playing.

127.t: Sir Oliver Bibbs, drummer and bandleader in Chicago
127.s: Punch recalls working with drummer Sir Oliver Bibbs at Chicago clubs and in Springfield; Allen asks about his leaving Chicago.
127.q: Now I tell you another fella I forgot about. I was making a record. He didn't make no. You might have heard of him, but I wasn't in a long time. Sir Oliver Bibbs. Sir Oliver Bibbs. Yeah, that's where he'd give his name. I waited with him in Chicago at the club silhouette. I waited at the Gehrig…

127.t: The Tenderloin district and Freddie Keppard at the Dreamland
127.s: Punch played blues in the district; he did not know Jelly Roll, Tony Jackson or Oliver there but worked with Keppard and Doc Cook in Chicago.
127.q: The district. Oh hell yeah man. You was. I was playing with a fellow and Ken Beard in the daytime. Cans of the women, you know, the whole hustle of them. 10 cents a can and every night I'd get up there and play the blues with the piano player. Now he, I forget his name, he died. He was a sickly…

127.t: The Golden Lily band under Francois Mosley
127.s: Five years at a Chicago spot until a fire; he names the band and Ted Wilson.
127.q: But we had a lovely band at the Golden Lill in Chicago. We had five years, like one spot. A boy named little Francois Mosley had the band, and the place caught a fire on a Saturday night. That's how we got out of job there. But we would have been there, I guess, for 10 years. That was a nice job.

127.t: Joining Tiny Parham at the Dreamland
127.s: Cliff Jones recruited him for Parham's band at the Dreamland; he names the sidemen.
127.q: And this Cliff Jones, we call him Snag, he come up one day to my house and told me that Tiny Paar sent him to get me to play with him. So I went on down and made rehearsal with him and went through okay. So I went there at the Dreamland with him and then tell the truth, we come on down there and…

127.t: Hugh Swift's band at Jeffery Tavern
127.s: He joined Swift's sixteen-piece radio band, recommended by Junior Cobbs, and was featured singing and playing.
127.q: Now, about the first real job I went on in Chicago, many people don't know it, but we were supposed to be the first band that went on the air. A fellow by the name of Hugh Swift. Oh, yeah. He had 16 pieces out of the place. They called Jeffrey Tavern. Chicago and Jeffrey.

127.t: Playing in the same brass band as Louis; meeting in Chicago
127.s: Punch and Louis played in the same brass band; they met in Chicago after Punch left New Orleans in 1927, and Louis put him with a band on Sundays.
127.q: Well, how about that? We can get on to it, but you got all that stuff.

127.t: Earl Hines, Jabo Smith and Al Wynn
127.s: One night with Hines replacing Jabo Smith; first played with Al Wynn in Chicago.
127.q: Yeah, Jabo Smith. I worked with him one night and Jabo come back the next night. That was his job. He just got off somewhere and didn't show up.

92.t: Forming and playing in Roy Eldridge's band at the Three Deuces
92.s: After Eldridge left Henderson he formed a small band in Chicago with Collins, Dave Young, Scoops Carey, Zutty Singleton and Truck Parham, staying about three years.
92.ch: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
92.q: Roy was at the Grand Terrace with Fletcher Henderson, he and Chu Berry. So Roy formed this band that I was in Roy's band.

92.t: Playing with Stuff Smith in Chicago
92.s: Collins haunted Stuff Smith's hotel group with Bernard Addison, Cozy Cole and John Brown and jammed with them in the dressing room.
92.ch: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
92.q: see, it was about '59. Yeah, around that time, just before Stuff Smith died. And Stuff Smith, there was a giant. And I used to play with him quite a bit in Chicago. He used to come to Chicago to play the hotels, and I would just haunt him, and he had a guitarist by the name of Bernard Addison at…

92.t: Black bands in Chicago hotels were the exception
92.s: Willard and Collins discuss how black bands rarely played Chicago hotels, such as the Hotel La Salle, and mention Eddie South behind a screen.
92.ch: Fourteen years with Nat Cole and the recording sessions
92.q: That's right, yeah. Well, this was the exception, it wasn't the rule. And I would go down just to be there because these were great musicians, and you know how as a youngster I wanted to be heard too. So this is why my first contact and meeting with Stuff. So when he worked with us with Nat it was…

92.s: He met Johnson in Chicago in the early thirties and heard him in after-hours spots, ranking him with Lester Young and Ben Webster.
92.ch: Haiti, Artie Shaw and Los Angeles work
92.q: Yeah, but this is -- this was New York. And speaking of going back to New York, returning, I always see musicians who I've worked with and I have beautiful memories working with. I saw Bud Johnson, who I've known for years and years. I met Bud in Chicago, oh, in the early thirties, actually. Bud…

92.t: Scoops Carey: saxophonist turned Chicago lawyer
92.s: Collins came up with Carey, who joined Tatum's sextet at the same time, played with Earl Hines, then became a lawyer and died of cancer.
92.ch: Chicago, the Woodside, the army and 52nd Street
92.q: Had tremendous technique, very big sound. He was with Earl Hines, he did some very good things. He was with Earl Hines for quite a while. But we played around Chicago, we had a band around -- we had a little band around Chicago, and we joined Art Tatum at the same time. The Scoops was like a…

92.t: Ray Nance's Chicago band in 1932 and Lena Horne's arrival
92.s: Collins heard Nance's band at Dave's, played in Nance's big band, and once saw a beautiful Lena Horne step off Noble Sissle's bus.
92.ch: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
92.q: I didn't play with his high school band, I was in school with him. He had another guitarist, a marvelous guitarist by the name of Claude Adams. Claude died very young but Ray always had very good bands. And I played with him later in a big band, and --

92.t: Segregation in Chicago clubs and restaurants
92.s: The Three Deuces took only white patrons and Chicago was prejudiced about restaurants and hotels, which Collins says changed during World War II.
92.ch: Chicago: Henderson, Tatum and Roy Eldridge, then New York and the army
92.q: State and Wacker. Wacker Drive and State Street, in the basement. But no black musicians could come there, you know, clientele, no patrons, black patrons could come there. They'd get run out of there. This was Chicago at that time. It was a terrible -- Chicago really started -- I think the blacks…

427.t: Back in Chicago and Little Bo's band again
427.s: He tells of the Blue Room and meeting up again with Little Bo's fifteen-piece band and Sheila Guys.
427.ch: Carnegie Hall and the touring years
427.q: So I had to come out here, see about my place o' business. So I had my sister runnin' it for me. 'Course, in the meantime, I went to Chicago. I lived seventeen years in Chicago. I got married in Chicago to a lady called Louella Brown. So we got together...Cut it off [the tape recorder].

427.t: Pete Johnson visits; staying in Chicago and playing a club under the El
427.s: Louella persuaded them to stay in Chicago and found them a job at Johnny's Place, with a naked woman painted on the window.
427.q: So I told him, "Come on over an' see my new house." "That ain't nome o' your house." I say, "That what the man say." I say, "I put my name on it. My wife got her name on it." He was jealous: "You a lucky dude. You is lucky. You sumpin' else!" I said, "Well, you're now lookin' at a married man."…

427.t: Working Ethel Waters' club and meeting Louella
427.s: He and Pete Johnson worked Waters' Chicago club; Louella, a flower girl, bought him ties.
427.q: So, I came to Chicago. Had one place I hadn't played. I'd been skippin' all aroun' Chicago. So we went...I started workin' in a place that Ethel Waters owned...in a nightclub. Pete Johnson and myself, we got a job at Ethel Waters's nightclub. So, the meantime, we was goin' to another club where…

427.t: Louella in a veil, and the invitation to the Club DeLisa
427.s: He didn't recognize her dressed up, talked with her at the bar, and she urged him to try her club.
427.q: So she was sittin' up there drinkin' a champagne. She didn't drink but she was just sippin' on some champagne. So she looked good so I turned...so I just...mosey on over and see who this is. So when I got over there to her, (she) said, "You don't remember me?"

427.t: Ethel Waters owned the Chicago club but her boyfriend ran it
427.s: Waters rarely appeared and Turner would not name her boyfriend.
427.q: She just owned the club. She never was there half the time. Her boyfriend run the joint.

427.t: An all-night outing and card game with Pete Johnson
427.s: After the show they ate Italian food, watched the five a.m. show, and played cards until afternoon.
427.q: I say, "Well, this is luck 'cause cabs kinda hard to get... scarce in the mornin' about two o'clock." So I said, "Well, you made up your mind you gonna go over to the club with me?" Say, "I ain't ready to go to bed. It's too lonesome in my house...in my room...by myself." I said, "I don't sleep…

427.t: Winters in Detroit clubs and the Club DeLisa again
427.s: He worked the Zombie Club and Sportry's Bar in Detroit, where a stage sat over the bar, then Chicago's Club DeLisa.
427.ch: Washington, New Orleans and the road
427.q: An' I got through runnin' around with that...went back to Chicago, stayed the winter, then I headed back out in the summertime. In the meantime, in the wintertime, I play all up in Detroit, Michigan. Had a club up there called the Zombie Club. Had a club called Sportry's (?) Bar. I used to wrrk…

270.t: Jazz Limited in Chicago and the guitarist Mike
270.s: He worked at Jazz Limited in Chicago and recalls an older versatile guitarist named Mike.
270.q: I took a fellow named Mike, he was a very versatile man like me. He played guitar in bands and sang, and he was older than me. He was down here when Louis Armstrong came to me on you somewhere in the 30 and played somewhere out there in the middle.

270.t: Chicago combo work: the Chocolate Music Bars hotel tours
270.s: In Chicago he moved to combos and formed the Chocolate Music Bars, touring hotel and cocktail jobs in the Midwest.
270.q: Well, I got away from bands. They had a lot of three pieces, four pieces of combo in the yard. And I got with a fellow named Melvin Banks and we got with a fellow named John Creech, Papa John Creech, he played up at the Roses. And we organized a group, we called ourselves the Chocolate Music Balls.…

270.t: Moving to Chicago and electric guitar
270.s: After the season ends in St. Louis he visits a friend in Chicago, settles in 1938, marries, and gets work as an electric guitarist.
270.q: His name was Joe Bradford, a friend of mine, so I wrote a term, he told me, yes, come on up, see, so he was married and he had two daughters, and one of the girls was born while I was staying with him, so he made it so pleasant and so nice for me, like, saying I didn't have to pay a whole lot of…

270.t: The Chicago trio and the Chocolate Bar of Music
270.s: How his trio formed, got its name at the Bar of Music, toured Midwest hotels, and broke up around 1946; later small groups.
270.q: Well, this trio started, we started from a band with, uh, Oliver Beathen, I forget, he had a, some book ahead of gave him a contract to go on the road, and we used to hush around at, uh, the local in Chicago, and it was about, uh, 10 or 15 piece band, but when they, and, uh, the bass player and the…

270.t: Chicago trio length, guitar versus banjo, his brother
270.s: The Chicago trio was his longest group; he played electric guitar and returned to banjo only in the mid-1950s. His oldest brother played banjo in Robert Clark's band.
270.q: Well, we started up, I'd say around about, oh, around about 40, and we stayed together, I think, about 44, 45, maybe part of 46.

270.t: Danny Barker, the Chicago excursion and the offers Sayles turned down
270.s: He recommends Danny Barker for Albert's job, tells how Barker met his uncle Paul and went to Chicago, calls it a missed break, then returns to Desvigne's band living near Randy Hall.
270.ch: Desvigne, Chicago offers and Peter Hone's band
270.q: Yeah, had a woman piano player. I'm trying to think of her name. I know that woman well. She lived there on any street near Claiborne.

287.t: Leaving for Chicago in 1929 and hearing the New Orleans men there
287.s: He went to Chicago alone in 1929 and auditioned for Decca. He heard Louis Armstrong at the Sunset and Oliver at the Plantation and was nervous when asked to sit in.
287.q: Well, I had to play in with different combinations and I had a chance to audition for some recording. What company was that? That was Decker.

287.t: Chicago bands, Fazola, and the Oliver band at the Plantation
287.s: He lists organized Chicago bands and notes Fazola with Bob Crosby. The Oliver band at the Plantation was a real New Orleans cabaret band, packed nightly, with Oliver stomping his foot to start tunes.
287.q: Tension to. Yeah. At the time, whenever Bob Cross would come through there, and his band like Fazola, Clarinet, and he's from New Orleans.

287.t: Playing on the Navy Pier excursion boat and Clark Street
287.s: He led a four-piece band of New Orleans men on a Navy Pier excursion boat and played Clark Street, where white Chicago musicians were playing jazz. He does not recall Tom Brown.
287.q: You mean here or in Chicago? Well, both here and in Chicago. Well, I used to play on a boat in Chicago at the Navy Pier. That's a recreation pier that extends about a mile, I think, out in Lake Michigan. I used to play on a little excursion boat that makes trips from the pier for a half hour. I…

287.t: Playing blues at the Firehouse on Clark Street for white jazz fans
287.s: On Clark Street he played the blues all night for white fans who came to hear New Orleans blues, some of whom sat in. He does not recall their names, and notes record collectors.
287.ch: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
287.q: Well, I was in Chicago, playing with different bunches, you know what I mean? I played on Clark Street at the Firehouse. Many jazz fans used to come there and have me to play the blues all night. They'd come in, I mean white jazz fans, they'd come in and treat me well, just to hear the blues. Of…

287.t: Sitting in with Bob Crosby's band
287.s: He saw no famous Chicago sessions except Bob Crosby's. Crosby's crew chartered his excursion boat, then he and Oliver Alcorn jammed with them, his only time with Crosby.
287.ch: Chicago years: recordings, Armstrong, wartime exit
287.q: The only one I was present at was Bob Crossby. They had a recording session before us. We came on after them, and them fellas was really small guys. They had a case of scotch and soda, and they had heard a whole lot of talk of the Harlem Ham Fats, so they invited us in the studio, and we drank,…

287.t: Chicago jazz mixed with local musicians; why New Orleans men moved north
287.s: Jazz in Chicago was played by New Orleans men mixed with readers who could not play without music. Musicians left as New Orleans work slowed and Storyville closed.
287.q: Well, just like I told you, there wasn't many jazz bands. All this jazz in Chicago was played by the musicians from New Orleans. And then they'd be mixed up with Chicago musicians and you can't very well play like you want. With certain numbers they wouldn't know. And most of them read music. They…

0.t: The Simeon brothers and the Chicago cabarets young clarinetists haunted
0.s: Omer Simeon started clarinet in Chicago; the young clarinet players went to the Royal Garden, Dreamland and other cabarets to hear Oliver, Noone and others.
0.q: Very quiet fellow. Both of them Simeons are play, Simeon, a very beautiful fellows. We used to hang out at the -- we clarinet players -- every night we could, we'd put on long pants and go in the cabaret, like the Royal Garden, where Joe Oliver was Earl Gardner, Oliver Willis and like Jimmy Noonan…

0.t: Why Chicago led New York in cabarets and night life
0.s: Chicago was the cabaret center of the country around 1922, with a concentrated black population.
0.ch: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
0.q: No, didn't do any harm. No, because it's so -- of course, Chicago was so far ahead of New York at that time for night life because every corner you had a club, after hour joints, you know. Like, for instance—

0.t: Map of the South Side cabarets: Dreamland, Sunset, Columbia Tavern
0.s: Caldwell lists the cabarets and after-hours places along State Street from 31st to 35th, and who led the bands.
0.ch: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
0.q: No, they were all up -- these big clubs were mostly outside of Dreamland. Dreamland was on State Street between 35th and 36th.

0.t: A black entertainment district and the white audience uptown
0.s: Entertainment was concentrated in a mostly black area from 31st to 47th Street, with ballrooms and armories, and white patrons came to the ritzier places as in Harlem.
0.ch: Chicago's South Side night life in the early 1920s
0.q: Yes, it was, from 31st and State all the way up to 47th Street. Of course, they had a lot of little theaters, like between -- like the Pickford Theater on -- between Michigan Avenue and Indiana Avenue. See, at that time like Michigan was Michigan Boulevard then when I was a kid because like the J.…

0.t: Sitting in at the Sunset and copying Buster Bailey's solo
0.s: He sat in at the Sunset Cafe and played Buster Bailey's 'Tootsie Goodbye' solo note for note, to Rudy Jackson's amusement; the band was Carroll Dickerson's.
0.q: He really did. Yeah, I appreciate it. Funny thing about it, though, it was -- he was working with -- with this band down at the Sunset. So Simcan and I and Cecil Trwin Aaron, we all go and listen to the clarinet players, like Jimmy Noon, Buster Bailey and the different ones, you know. So Buster…

0.t: Leaving the Tavern band for Bernie Young; Dolly Jones as leader
0.s: Bernie Young organised his own recording band and Caldwell left the Tavern, whose band belonged to trumpeter Dolly Jones.
0.ch: National Guard band and first jobs in Chicago
0.q: Bernie, he organized, he took us out of that group and organized his own band for recording and playing. I left then.. I left that group at the Tavern and joined Bernie Young.

758.t: Leading the Three Deuces band with Zutty
758.s: Roy took a leader job at the Three Deuces with Zutty's group, added Joe, and the broadcast wire made the club a hangout.
758.q: : Because they'd been trying to get... Me and Chu used to go the Three Deuces and jam. The only reason we went down there is because we used to get good ribs there. And it was nice playing. Art was working there. Zutty had a group down there, and I think Vernell York(?) was working with him.

758.t: Meeting Jo Jones and Prez in Chicago
758.s: Roy befriended Prez and Jo Jones in Chicago, picking them up in his new Ford Roadster after work.
758.q: : Yeah. Well, going back to the Three Deuces thing, that's when I first met Jo Jones. Prez I knew from when I was with McKinney's Cotton Pickers in Baltimore, you know.

758.t: Chicago after-hours clubs and Dorothy Donegan
758.s: Roy recalls Chicago clubs, breakfast dances, and Dorothy Donegan sitting in.
758.q: : We used to work at Anise(?) Club, too. I used to go down there and stop there and play with a guy that's a lawyer, a trumpet player. He's on Louis Armstrong's (?). I'm trying to think of his name.

758.t: Teddy flips; Gabby joins on piano
758.s: After Teddy Wilson flipped, Roy hired Gabby and headed to Buckeye Lake.
758.q: : Well, Gabby(?) was one of those type of cats, if you'd stop somewhere to get gas or something, he would go in there for like soda, you know, he could open the bottle and drink it down before you could bat your eyes. We played Columbus... No, we went from Columbus... Because we were on our way to…

758.t: Decca date, pneumonia and Harold West on drums
758.s: Roy made a Decca session, caught pneumonia, and replaced Zutty with Harold West, who could not read.
758.q: : I was working at the Deuces. But you see, I had one record contract with Decca. We made the one date, you know, with "After You've Gone" and that on it, and then they had the band. And buying(?) the band, I got pneumonia

758.t: Beating Earl Hines and the Christopher Columbus hit
758.s: The band outplayed Earl Hines at the Grand Terrace, made Christopher Columbus, and then publishing-driven arrangements led Roy to give notice.
758.q: : We got there and rehearsed, and things turned out real good. We did the sound... We played a battle of music the first night against Earl Hines. Tore him up, baby. Tore his group up. I'll tell you, it was so bad, that when you get... They had those jitneys in Chicago. When you'd get in the…

78.t: Chicago band members: Omar Simeon and Walter Fuller
78.s: Horace picks out Omar Simeon, a sight-reading first alto who once subbed in Fletcher's band, and trumpeter Walter Fuller who 'sold' a number like Basin Street.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: This particular picture we're looking at here now -- here's a guy you've got to know because he was one of the greats of jazz on the clarinet. He played a lot

78.t: Joining Fletcher at the Grand Terrace after Hawkins leaves for Europe
78.s: When his own band broke up Horace joined Fletcher at the Grand Terrace as pianist, bringing Crosby and Roy Eldridge. With Hawkins gone, Fletcher combined Chu Berry's swing and Elmer Williams' tone.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: I later joined Fletcher at the Grant Terrace when our band broke up. I joined Fletcher; I took Israel Crosby with me. I took Roy Eldridge with me, and Chu Berry was always there with Fletcher, and we had another tenor saxophonist. He was a great saxophonist. He just died recently -- named Elmer…

78.t: Chicago in the thirties: the 400 and 5100 Clubs, Ray Nance leaves for Ellington
78.s: Clarifies he went with Fletcher to Chicago, left to form his own band at Swingland, then returned. At the 5100 Club with Danny Thomas on the bill, violinist-trumpeter Ray Nance was persuaded to join Duke Ellington.
78.ch: Arranging for Fletcher, Goodman and Barnet
78.q: No, this was in the thirties. You know, Fletcher went to Chicago. In fact, he took his band into Chicago where and this was when I was with Fletcher, and I stayed with Fletcher, I believe, better than a year in Chicago, and this is when I formed my own band and went into Swingland, and Fletcher was…

78.t: Earl Hines, Ed Fox's Grand Terrace and Horace's 'Shufflin' Joe'
78.s: Ed Fox owned the Grand Terrace with Hines and later Fletcher. Walter Fuller got Horace to arrange for Hines, whose band had Omer Simeon, Jimmy Mundy and George Dixon, as straw boss; Horace wrote 'Shufflin' Joe'. He sums up the varied bandleaders.
78.ch: Arranging for other bandleaders and closing talk
78.q: Father Hines. Let's see. That takes us back to Chicago, the Grand Terrace, where he used to play, aong with Fletcher, you know. There was a guy named Ed Fox that owned the Grand Terrace in Chicago that had Earl Hines under contract, and later on he had Fletcher under contract. And, of course, the…

78.t: Swingland run, the Chicago union five-day week, Grand Terrace rivals
78.s: Swingland ran seven nights a week for three or four years on WBBM until bassist Harry Grey, later local president, won a five-day week. Ed Fox's Grand Terrace had Earl Hines and Fletcher; Lawrence Welk preceded them on air.
78.ch: Starting out in New York and Chicago
78.q: Until this union started in Chicago, and then we went down to five. My -- of course, my bass player at that time was a guy named Harry Grey who later became the President of the Musicians' Local in Chicago. There was two locals at that time -- local 10 and our local in Chicago. And Harry Grey was…

78.t: The 5100 Club in Chicago, Danny Thomas and broadcasts on WBBM
78.s: Following Mark Fisher at the 5100 Club in 1939-40, Horace led a big band behind Danny Thomas and talked the owner into WBBM broadcasts, with Fuller, Ray Nance, Peewee Jackson and Omer Simeon.
78.ch: Connie's Inn, Duke Ellington and the Swingland band
78.q: Mark. M-A-R-K. Mark Fisher. Well I followed his band into the 5100 Club, and this was around '39 and '40, and I played for a guy there named Harry [Eagle] who had Danny Thomas there as the star of the show. And from there, you know where Danny went.

256.t: Introduction and the telegram calling him to Chicago
256.s: Brunis introduces himself, gives his birth details, and tells how Rag Baby Stevens's wire brought Paul Mares and then him to Chicago and the Campbell Gardens.
256.q: Good morning ladies and gentlemen. This is George Brunus of the Musical Brunus Family of New Orleans. It's a little in the view, the gentleman would like to know, I was born New Orleans, the Irish Channel, February 6th, 1902. I'm now 56 years of age, going pretty strong for my age. I came up from…

256.t: First snow, Blatt's Palm Garden and boxing with Muggsy
256.s: He plays the first set, goes wild in his first snow, meets Jack Pettis, Frank Snyder, Elmer Schoebel and Muggsy at Blatt's, and is made to box Muggsy; then the move to Lincoln Gardens and a Streckfus boat offer.
256.q: Uh, Rag Baby, Paul, myself and Tramonist, piano player. I just can't recall the piano player. Oh God, yeah. So, uh, we played the first set and went over pretty good and ragged. And the boss, uh, Stein was very happy. So I happened to go outside and somebody said, it's snowing. So I wanted to see…

256.t: What Friars Inn was like and the gangsters who came in
256.s: A basement place on Wabash owned by Mike Fritzel, popular with hoods and entertainers.
256.q: It was in the basement on Wabash and Van Buren. It was owned by Mike Fritzl alone. No syndicate, no Jacobson. And, uh... Were there a lot of gangsters around? A lot of hoods in those days. Can I mention the names? Uh, yeah.

256.t: Rappolo, Bee Palmer's act and the first band at Friars Inn
256.s: Brunis recalls Rappolo's girlfriend, Bee Palmer's shimmy act, and who made up the first band at Friars Inn.
256.q: Well, he was working in Davenport somewhere, and he was going with this young, beautiful, blonde girl, and, uh, she, I think she was killed in an automobile accident.

256.t: Tom Brown's band and the Brown brothers' farmer costumes
256.s: The Brown brothers came to Chicago, Shields swapped jobs, and band members' trades.
256.q: Yellow Nunes came up with the original band, and they played on the Red Lantern. A guy by the name of Harry James brought them up here, not the trumpet players. Yes, yeah.

184.t: Following Tubby to Chicago in 1918 and the stockyard job
184.s: Tubby and others went to the Deluxe Cafe in Chicago; Hall and his parents were sent for, he walked off a stockyard job and took his brother's place when Tubby was drafted.
184.q: Yeah, they went up there, and they had a band at the Deluxe Cafe. Lawrence Dewey with them. That's right, I think Lawrence Dewey had a band at that time, yeah. So he was up there working with them at the Deluxe Cafe at 35th and State, a fellow by the name of Shaw. And so about later on my oldest…

184.t: The Dreamland band and how Oliver took over from Mutt Carey
184.s: Hall describes the Dreamland band with Sugar Johnny, Lil Hardin, Mutt Carey and Dodds, and how Oliver took the band while Carey was away in New Orleans.
184.q: Yeah, I wasn't quite old enough yet for the first draft. So when he went, I'd taken over, and in the meantime, I don't know what happened to Tuley Garland, but when I wound up, Breaux was playing bass, Wilmer Breaux. So that wound up with Wilmer Breaux, Sugar Johnny, Lawrence Dewey, Roy Palmer,…

184.t: Pekin gangsters, Al Capone and the Royal Garden
184.s: Working after hours at the Pekin ended amid shootings and gangsters, where he first saw Al Capone; Oliver then got work at the Royal Garden.
184.q: So we worked down there a while, then after that we got out of there, there was so much trouble down there, we lose that job, we close the place up I think. Yeah, there's some shooting on there. Yeah, there's some gangsters there. Yeah, there's some gangsters, that's right. Because that's the first…

184.t: When and why Tubby went to Chicago
184.s: They work out that Tubby went north in 1917 before Oliver, and joined the Deluxe Cafe band though he may not have gone to play music.
184.ch: Brass bands, lessons and Tubby's story
184.q: Oh yeah, oh yeah, I even went before Oliver did. That's right, you were up there. Or any of this. That's why I met him. I only came to go to the band.

184.t: Opening a Chicago club with Jimmy Noone and Earl Hines
184.s: Hall opened a club with Noone and Hines, and left after trouble with a married coat-check girl.
184.q: So finally I had a little run in with a girl there, you know, working in a check room and come to find out she was married. So that broke that up. So she started disturbing. At the meantime, Ora set for me to come to Los Angeles to work at a Texas dance hall, because the drummer they had had two…

875.t: Excursion trains to Chicago and meeting Louis Armstrong in 1929
875.s: Playing in the baggage car on excursion trains to Chicago, meeting Louis at Warwick Hall, and band members taken along.
875.q: When did you first meet Louis, speaking about him? The first time I met Louis to know him was in 1929 in Chicago at the Warwick Hall.

875.t: Eddie Johnson, Punch Miller and Lee Collins in Chicago
875.s: Other New Orleans musicians in Chicago, and a band contest against Lee Collins's band.
875.q: Did you know Lee Collins down here? Oh yeah. I know Lee used to play out there at the La Vida before I did. Lee played there a long time. Yeah I know Lee a long, long time ago.

875.t: Chicago excursion trains in the late 1920s
875.s: Howard recalls playing in the baggage car on the Chicago excursions from 1928 on, after Sam Morgan's band went first, and meeting Louis Armstrong at the hall.
875.q: And that's the first time that I remember Lewis because when Lewis was here I didn't know him. See, well he came over at the hall and I got to know him. Which is a fine, fine man and a crazy buddy kid.

875.t: The excursion band and how the Chicago jobs were arranged
875.s: Howard names the men he took north and explains that a railroad porter hired the band and arranged the Chicago dances.
875.q: The whole band went up there. Yeah, because I had taken Guy Kelly, which was a wonderful band, and I had taken a band, which was a wonderful trumpet man, you heard of him.

875.t: Playing on trucks in Chicago with Punch Miller
875.s: Howard tells how the excursion band advertised the dance on trucks at 47th and South Parkway, with Punch Miller jumping on to play.
875.q: Man, man, that was the time. That's the time, Lee was waking up at their story up on Ramport Street, and they went for some other people. And anyway.

50.t: First nightclub: the Plantation with King Oliver in Chicago
50.s: In 1925 she was struck by the watermelon decorations at the Plantation, where Albert Nicholas played with King Oliver.
50.ch: Family and early memories of Jelly
50.q: Yes, with King Oliver and the whole place was covered with artificial watermelons, you know made out of tissue paper Oh really? And I was so impressed with it, I really, in truth, I didn't hear the music looking up all the time Because I had never been in a nightclub before in my life Up on the…

50.t: Going to Chicago when Jelly was sick; his new car
50.s: He wrote he was sick, she came for three weeks and stayed a year; he borrowed a car and told her he was 28.
50.q: He was sick in Chicago. And it happened something like Walvash Street, Walvash Avenue, Walvash. He lived on Walvash and I lived on Everhart.

50.t: Staying at Mrs. Martin's; Ralph Scull and Ink Williams show her Chicago
50.s: She boarded with a religious family on Eberhart; Scull and Ink Williams took her sightseeing and said Jelly educated himself.
50.q: Yeah, Martin's. That's where I stayed with Mr. Martin's. Yeah, they were religious people, lovely people. And it was so nice because they were harvesting somewhere out in— out from Chicago, a lot of corn and stuff. They were canned and all that stuff. But I had never seen anybody canned anything in…

50.s: They compare the photo suit with the belted back and high button shoes.
50.q: Well, I mean, you see this suit here with these high button shoes and a belt behind his coat? They were wearing those kind of gabby clothes.

50.t: Length of her stay in Chicago
50.s: She arrived spring 1925 and left October or November to be home for her grandmother's birthday.
50.q: I went in the spring of 1925, right after all the snow was up, because he didn't want me to come during that winter. He was sick that winter, but he didn't want me to come. He didn't want me to come.

881.t: Oliver at the Royal Garden, Armstrong's arrival and 35th Street
881.s: He follows the Royal Garden bands, Oliver's move to Dave Peyton after the fire, Armstrong's arrival, and the cabarets along State and 35th Street.
881.q: He had the band. Yeah, I couldn't call his name just then. Yeah. And then right across the street was Joe Oliver played over there. Holly Powers did the singing. Joe was doubling, he was doubling at the Pekin. He'd leave the Dreamland and go to Pekin. And then later, at that time now, this Royal…

881.t: Chicago cabarets and bands of the early 1920s
881.s: Recalls the many Chicago places and bands: the Sunset, the Plantation, the Entertainers, the Deluxe, the Vendome, with Dutrey and Noone in various bands.
